provenance: FABRICATED. These rows describe no trained model and no real run. They exist to exercise engine 14's weighting rule, which cannot be exercised by the real leaderboard: the walk-forward trains one predictor per fold, so every real model version has exactly one row and every aggregation across folds gives the same answer. Every number below was chosen to make one property of the rule observable, and each row says which. Nothing here may be read as a measurement of anything.
rule_under_test: skill(fold) = max(0, 1 - brier / base_rate_brier); skill(version) = unweighted mean over that version's folds; weight = skill / sum(skill)

expected.note: Recomputed in the test from the rows rather than read from here. Written down only so a reader can see at a glance what the fixture is for; the test does not import these numbers.

rows.why: Two folds, so the unweighted mean across folds is actually computed. Skills 0.5 and 0.4 give a mean of 0.45; a most-recent-fold rule would give 0.4 and a fold-count-weighted mean would differ once another version had a different number of folds, so the three aggregations disagree here and agree on the real table.
The second fold of the same version. Skill 0.4.

SUPERSEDED DUPLICATE of the row below: same (model_id, model_version, fold), older updated_at, and a brier that would score 0.9 rather than 0.1. There is no unique index on those three columns, so duplicates are possible and B's leaderboard_entries deliberately returns every match rather than hiding a broken idempotency convention. If engine 14 averaged the two as though they were folds, or kept the older one, this version's weight would move a long way -- which is what makes the collapse observable rather than assumed.

The surviving row for that version: one fold, skill 0.1, so its weight is visibly smaller than the two-fold version's without being zero. A rule that clipped everything below some threshold, or that ranked rather than scaled, would not produce 0.1818.

Worse than its own base rate: brier 0.25 against a base rate of 0.2 gives a raw skill of -0.25, clipped to zero. Spec 97 requires such a version to get weight zero, and this is the row that proves it does. It must also NOT drag the other weights -- a rule that normalised over the unclipped -0.25 would push the other two above their true share, which is spec 97's first named mutation.

A SECOND MODEL FAMILY, and the best score in the file. Engine 14 weights only its own family, so this row must be excluded entirely -- included, its skill of 0.95 would dominate the normalisation and hand it most of the predictor's weight. There is one family on the real table today, which is exactly why weighting across families would have gone unnoticed. This is the row spec 97's 'at least two distinct model_ids' requirement is for.
